messages.subject: Re: Predictions INLA
parts:
Hi,

thanks for your email. There isn't anything strange going on: If x[i]
is not observed, it is simply integrated out conditioned on the data
that is observed. The values of NA is interpreted different if an
observation is NA or a component is NA,

y ~ 1 + x + f(idx)


if y[1] = NA, then its not observed so there is no likelihood
contribtion related to y[1]

if x[1] = NA, then there is no effect of x for linear.predictor[1], so
this is eqv to x[1] = 0

if idx[1] = NA, then there is no effect of 'f' for linear.preditor[1]


H


On Fri, 2018-06-29 at 13:44 +0200, Jaione Etxeberria wrote:
> Dear Håvard and INLA group,
> I’m Jaione Etxeberria from the Public University of Navarre (Spain).
> I wrote you some months ago with a question related to the way that
> INLA works with missing data in the response variable.
> In my particular example, I am analyzing the usefulness of a share
> component model (besag2 model) + another time and age-specific terms
> to analyze the incidence (as disease 1) and mortality (as disease 2)
> of the same cancer location. In my particular data set, the mortality
> is observed in the period 1990-2008 (all areas) while the incidence
> is observed in the period 1990-2005 (all areas).
> Using the model I mentioned before, I am able to predict incidence
> data in the period 2006-2008 by area. At this point, my question is
> how does INLA estimate/ predict these results. I am not an expert in
> Bayesian field and maybe this is a trivial thing, but I do not really
> understand what INLA does predict NA values. Is there any paper or
> book in which this issue is tackled?
> Many, many thanks in advance!
> Jaione Etxeberria.
